entities.name: Voice over IP
entities.label: Idea
entities.summary:
Voice over Internet Protocol (VoIP) fundamentally reshaped global telecommunications in the late 20th and early 21st centuries, transforming the transmission of human speech from circuit-switched telephone networks to packet-switched data networks. Emerging from foundational research in computer networking during the Cold War, particularly the development of ARPANET, VoIP leveraged the burgeoning Internet to digitize and encapsulate voice signals into data packets. This innovation democratized long-distance communication, drastically reducing costs and fostering new forms of digital interaction, ultimately challenging the entrenched monopolies of traditional telephony and accelerating the convergence of voice and data services worldwide.

The conceptual underpinnings of VoIP trace back to early packet voice experiments in the 1970s, notably at USC's Information Sciences Institute (ISI) and MIT Lincoln Laboratory, which demonstrated the feasibility of transmitting real-time voice over ARPANET. Commercialization began in the mid-1990s with companies like VocalTec, which released the first internet phone software in 1995, allowing PC-to-PC voice calls. The subsequent standardization efforts by the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) through protocols like H.323 and SIP (Session Initiation Protocol) in the late 1990s were crucial, enabling interoperability and paving the way for widespread adoption. By the early 2000s, services like Skype (launched 2003) brought VoIP to the mainstream consumer, offering free or low-cost international calls.
